citations.quote:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). For a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ put $I_\alpha:=\{\mathbf i:
\mathbf i\text{ is a permutation of }\alpha\}$ and
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 11), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves the centrality, idempotency and orthogonality of the sums
$e_\alpha$ and then uses only those properties; primitivity and
exhaustiveness are recorded from the cited block theorem, not re-proved here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i,\alpha}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$ put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $H\le G$ be finite groups and let $k$ be any field. For every left
$kH$-module $M$ the map
$$\Phi_M:\ \operatorname{Ind}_H^G M=kG\otimes_{kH}M\longrightarrow\operatorname{Coind}_H^G M=\operatorname{Hom}_{kH}(kG,M),\qquad \Phi_M(g\otimes m)(x)=\begin{cases}(xg)m,&xg\in H,\\ 0,&xg\notin H,\end{cases}$$
is a natural isomorphism of $kG$-modules
([[def-restriction-induction-and-coinduction-for-group-modules]]). Consequently
$\operatorname{Ind}_H^G\cong\operatorname{Coind}_H^G$ naturally, so induction
is both a left and a right adjoint of restriction
([[thm-induction-is-left-adjoint-and-coinduction-right-adjoint-to-restriction]])
and is exact. No hypothesis on the characteristic of $k$, on splitting
fields, or on the prime $2$ is needed, and the argument is choice-free: it
uses only the finite selection of least representatives of the finitely many
left cosets.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$, $\mu$ a $p$-restricted partition
of $d$ and $A$ a removable $i$-node of $\mu$ such that $\nu=\mu\setminus A$
is again $p$-restricted; let $D(\mu)$ be the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$ in the dual-Specht (cellular) convention, so that
$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$
([[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]],
[[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]]), and let
$E_i$ be the residue-summand functor of
[[def-generalized-jm-primary-idempotents-and-residue-summand-functors]]. Then
$$[\,E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=0$$
if $A$ is not a normal $i$-node of $\mu$, and
$$[\,E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)\,]=\#\{B:\ B\ \text{normal }i\text{-node of }\mu\text{ weakly below }A\}$$
(counting $A$ itself) if $A$ is normal. The corresponding
Specht-to-restriction Hom criterion (Brundan 1998 Theorem 2.5, equivalently
Kleshchev II Theorem 0.4) is a distinct statement and is not asserted here.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence a terminal word is
$+^a0^c-^b$ for some $a,b,c\ge0$. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. A
terminating and locally confluent rewriting relation is confluent, so the
terminal word is unique; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has no $i$-nodes and empty signature, with
$\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for all $i$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

derivations.claim: The functor $F_i$ and duality. By [F1] each $F_i$ is a direct summand of induction with idempotent projection $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ invariant under the antipode; by [F2] induction is both a left and a right adjoint of restriction, hence $F_i$ is, up to the contragredient duality, both a left and a right adjoint of the corresponding residue restriction $E_i$. u=(1,1)$. The $1$-nodes of $\mu$ are the addable nodes $(1,2)$ and $(2,1)$, ordered top to bottom, so the reduced $1$-signature is $(+,+)$ and both nodes are conormal; the count of conormal $1$-nodes weakly above $B$ is $2$. The functor computation gives $F_1D(1)=kS_2e\otimes_{kS_1}k$ with $e=e((0,1))=P_{1,0}P_{2,1}=1$ in characteristic $2$, so $F_1D(1)\cong kS_2$ is the regular module, whose composition multiplicity of the trivial simple module $D(1,1)$ is $2$; this matches the count. The example also shows that the naive unshifted identity $[F_iD(\mu):D(
u)]=[E_iD(
u):D(\mu)]$ is *false* in general in positive characteristic: here $[E_1D(1,1):D(1)]=1
e2$, so the dually stated transfer of step 1.1, and not that identity, is what the proof uses.

Step 2.1 gives the two stated values of the multiplicity from the recorded theorem and its dual transfer; step 2.2 checks it in the smallest nontrivial characteristic-$2$ case and records the failure of the naive transfer identity. Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted
partition of $d\ge1$; write $D(\mu)$ for the simple $kS_d$-module labelled by
$\mu$
([[thm-modular-simple-modules-of-sn-are-the-p-regular-specht-heads]],
[[prop-p-regular-and-p-restricted-simple-labels-are-related-by-conjugate-sign-duality]]).
Let $A_i$ denote the good $i$-node of $\mu$, for those
$i\in\mathbb Z/p$ with $\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]). Then
$$\operatorname{soc}_{S_{d-1}}\bigl(D(\mu){\downarrow}_{S_{d-1}}\bigr)=\bigoplus_{i:\,\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0}D(\mu\setminus A_i),$$
a multiplicity-free sum over distinct simple modules: distinct residues give
distinct summands. The sum runs over the residues $i$ with
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, one good node per such residue; the completely
reducible special case (the restriction is semisimple if and only if every
normal node is good, Kleshchev II Theorem 0.6) is a separate statement and is
not asserted here.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). For a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ put $I_\alpha:=\{\mathbf i:
\mathbf i\text{ is a permutation of }\alpha\}$ and
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 11), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves the centrality, idempotency and orthogonality of the sums
$e_\alpha$ and then uses only those properties; primitivity and
exhaustiveness are recorded from the cited block theorem, not re-proved here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i,\alpha}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$ put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). For a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ put $I_\alpha:=\{\mathbf i:
\mathbf i\text{ is a permutation of }\alpha\}$ and
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 11), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves the centrality, idempotency and orthogonality of the sums
$e_\alpha$ and then uses only those properties; primitivity and
exhaustiveness are recorded from the cited block theorem, not re-proved here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i,\alpha}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$

$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$

$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$ put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.

and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $A$ be a finite-dimensional algebra and $M$ a finite-dimensional left
$A$-module.

- Its **radical** is
  $$   \operatorname{rad}(M)=J(A)M,   $$
  equivalently the intersection of the maximal submodules, by
  [[thm-module-radical-is-jacobson-radical-times-the-module]].

- Its **socle** $\operatorname{Soc}(M)$ is the sum of all simple submodules, as
  in [[def-socle-of-a-module]].

- Its **head** or **top** is the quotient
  $$   \operatorname{hd}(M):=M/\operatorname{rad}(M),   $$
  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers
  $\operatorname{rad}^i(M)/\operatorname{rad}^{i+1}(M)$.

The simple subquotients appearing in the Loewy layers are simple in the sense
of [[def-simple-module]].

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

**Well-definedness.** Each reduction step deletes two nonzero entries, so any
sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence a terminal word is
$+^a0^c-^b$ for some $a,b,c\ge0$. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. A
terminating and locally confluent rewriting relation is confluent, so the
terminal word is unique; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has no $i$-nodes and empty signature, with
$\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for all $i$.

**Convention warning.** The residue $c-r$ used here is the negative of
Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

boundaries.reason: The hypothesis ε_i(μ) > 0 excludes μ = ∅ and rank 0: the empty partition has no removable node, so no good node exists and the theorem’s hypothesis fails.

boundaries.evidence: Multiplicity zero does not occur under the hypothesis: by step 2.1 the multiplicity is ε_i(μ) ≥ 1; the good-node factor must occur, which is part of the content of the theorem.
The minimal case ε_i(μ) = 1 gives multiplicity 1 with simple socle and head D(ν); step 1.1 covers the single summand and step 2.1 the count.

p = 2 is included by the recorded source statement [F1] and by the duality argument of step 2.2, which uses only antipode invariance and self-duality; the statement imposes no characteristic restriction.
Socle and head are exactly the two endpoints of E_iD(μ); steps 1.1 and 2.2 compute them as D(ν), and step 3.1 records that the middle Loewy layers are left unspecified.
No choice is made: the good node of each residue is unique (step 1.1) and the module E_iD(μ) is fixed by the idempotent decomposition of step 1.1.

boundaries.reason: The theorem states that the good node gives a simple socle and head with total multiplicity ε_i(μ); it is not a biconditional, so there is no forward implication to check.
No converse is asserted: the theorem does not claim that a simple socle of E_iD(μ) forces A to be the good node, only the implication from the good node to the socle and head.

derivations.claim: Socle. By [F5] the socle of $\operatorname{Res}D(\mu)=\bigoplus_jE_jD(\mu)$ is $\bigoplus_j\operatorname{soc}(E_jD(\mu))$. By [F1] the socle of the restriction is the multiplicity-free sum of the $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ over the good nodes, and by [F2] each summand $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ lies in $E_jD(\mu)$ with its residue $j$; since a nonzero submodule of $E_jD(\mu)$ cannot lie in $\bigoplus_{l\ne j}E_lD(\mu)$ by the directness of the sum, the $j$-summand of the socle is exactly the single simple module $D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ and $\operatorname{soc}(E_jD(\mu))=D(\mu\setminus A_j)$ is simple. For $j=i$ this gives $\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu))=D(\mu\setminus A)=D(\nu)$.

Multiplicity. Applying the normal-node theorem [F3] with $X=A$: since $A$ is a normal $i$-node, $[E_iD(\mu):D(\nu)]$ is the number of normal $i$-nodes of $\mu$ weakly below $A$ counting $A$; by [F6] this is $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$.

Head. By [F4] the module $E_iD(\mu)$ is self-dual; by [F5] its head is the dual of its socle, $\operatorname{hd}(E_iD(\mu))\cong(\operatorname{soc}(E_iD(\mu)))^*$, which by step 1.1 is $D(
u)^*\cong D(
u)$ because $D(
u)$ is self-dual by [F4]. Hence the head is simple and isomorphic to $D(
u)$.

Conclusion. Step 1.1 gives simple socle $D(
u)$, step 2.1 the total multiplicity $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ of $D(
u)$ in $E_iD(\mu)$, and step 2.2 simple head $D(
u)$. The additional normal-node composition factors of [F3] may occur in the middle Loewy layers; the statement asserts only the endpoints and the total multiplicity, and no graded shift is displayed before the Hecke/KLR bridge.

On the set of $p$-restricted partitions
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]]) define partial operators
$\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ by
$$\tilde e_i\mu:=\mu\setminus A\quad\text{if }\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $A$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]), the
operator being undefined on $\mu$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; and
$$\tilde f_i\mu:=\mu\cup B\quad\text{if }\varphi_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on
$\mu$ when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. Then
$$\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$$
for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$; in particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$
are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one
and each $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one, and at most one good and at most
one cogood node exist in each residue. No module-theoretic statement is made
here: this item is pure combinatorics, and the identification of these
operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is a theorem
of the later Fock-space page, not an input here.

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$ and let $L_1,\dots,L_n\in kS_n$
be the Jucys-Murphy elements $L_r=\sum_{s<r}(s,r)$ of the symmetric group
algebra ([[def-jucys-murphy-elements-of-the-symmetric-group-algebra]]). Recall
that they commute pairwise
([[cor-jucys-murphy-elements-commute-pairwise]]), and for $r\le n$ the
element $L_r$ lies in the subalgebra $kS_r\subseteq kS_n$ and therefore
commutes with $S_{r-1}$.

**(i) Primary idempotents.** In the commutative subalgebra
$k[L_1,\dots,L_n]\subseteq kS_n$ the minimal polynomial of each $L_r$ on the
regular module splits into linear factors $X-a$ with $a$ in the prime field
$\mathbb F_p\subseteq k$, and the commuting family admits the following
simultaneous primary decomposition. There are pairwise orthogonal idempotents
$P_{r,a}\in k[L_r]\subseteq k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$, indexed by $r\in\{1,\dots,n\}$
and $a\in\mathbb F_p$, with
$$\sum_{a\in\mathbb F_p}P_{r,a}=1,\qquad P_{r,a}P_{r,b}=\delta_{a,b}P_{r,a},$$
such that for every finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module $M$ the action of
$P_{r,a}$ on $M$ is the projection onto the generalized eigenspace
$M_{r,a}=\{m\in M:(L_r-a)^Nm=0\text{ for }N\gg0\}$. The $P_{r,a}$ for
different $r$ commute, and for each sequence $\mathbf i=(i_1,\dots,i_n)$
with entries in $\mathbb F_p$ the products
$$e(\mathbf i):=\prod_{r=1}^nP_{r,i_r}\ \in\ k[L_1,\dots,L_n]$$
are pairwise orthogonal idempotents with $\sum_{\mathbf i}e(\mathbf i)=1$ and
$e(\mathbf i)M=M_{\mathbf i}$, the simultaneous generalized weight space
$M_{\mathbf i}=\{m:(L_r-i_r)^Nm=0\ \forall r,\ N\gg0\}$. Every $P_{r,a}$ and
every $e(\mathbf i)$ is fixed by the antipode $g\mapsto g^{-1}$ of $kS_n$.

**(ii) Content sums and blocks.** The symmetric group $S_n$ permutes the
coordinates of sequences, and two sequences are called *equivalent* when they
differ by a permutation, i.e. when they have the same content (the same
multiset of entries of $\mathbb F_p$). For a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^n$ put $I_\alpha:=\{\mathbf i:
\mathbf i\text{ is a permutation of }\alpha\}$ and
$$e_\alpha:=\sum_{\mathbf i\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf i)\ \in\ kS_n .$$
Each $e_\alpha$ is a central idempotent of $kS_n$, and distinct $e_\alpha$
are orthogonal; the nonzero $e_\alpha$ are exactly the primitive central
idempotents, that is the block idempotents of $kS_n$
([[def-p-blocks-by-primitive-central-idempotents]]), and every block
idempotent of $kS_n$ is of the form $e_\alpha$: this last identification of
the content sums with the blocks is the block theorem of Lyle-Mathas and
Brundan recorded as (2.41) in Kleshchev's survey (printed p. 11), with the
content of the block being the content of any of its partitions. The present
item proves the centrality, idempotency and orthogonality of the sums
$e_\alpha$ and then uses only those properties; primitivity and
exhaustiveness are recorded from the cited block theorem, not re-proved here.

**(iii) Residue-summand functors.** For a finite-dimensional $kS_n$-module
$M$, a residue $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and a content vector
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}$, put
$$e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}:=\sum_{\mathbf j\in I_\alpha}e((\mathbf j,i)) \ =\ e_\alpha^{(n-1)}\,P_{n,i},$$
where $(\mathbf j,i)$ denotes concatenation, $e_\alpha^{(n-1)}=\sum_{\mathbf
j\in I_\alpha}e(\mathbf j)$ is the content sum computed in $kS_{n-1}$ and
regarded in $kS_n$ through the inclusion $kS_{n-1}\subseteq kS_n$, and
$P_{n,i}\in k[L_n]$. Each $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}$ is an idempotent of $kS_n$
commuting with $kS_{n-1}$, the family
$\{e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\}_{i,\alpha}$ is a family of pairwise orthogonal
idempotents with $\sum_{i,\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=1$, and
$$E_iM:=\sum_{\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^{n-1}}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M =\bigoplus_{\alpha}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}M$$
is a $kS_{n-1}$-submodule of the restricted module with
$$\operatorname{Res}^{S_n}_{S_{n-1}}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}E_iM .$$
Dually, for a finite-dimensional $kS_d$-module $M$ of content
$\alpha\in(\mathbb Z/p)^d$, i.e. $M=e_\alpha^{(d)}M$, put
$$F_iM:=kS_{d+1}\,e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}M \qquad(i\in\mathbb Z/p),$$
with $e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}=e_\alpha^{(d)}P_{d+1,i}\in kS_{d+1}$; for a
general finite-dimensional $M$ put
$F_iM:=\bigoplus_\alpha kS_{d+1}e_{\alpha,\alpha_i}\otimes_{kS_d}e_\alpha M$.
Then $\operatorname{Ind}^{S_{d+1}}_{S_d}M=\bigoplus_{i\in\mathbb Z/p}F_iM$,
and all the functors $E_i,F_i$ are additive and exact, preserve
finite-dimensionality, and commute with contragredient duality, because the
projectors are fixed by the antipode. All statements hold at $p=2$; the
construction is choice-free.

Let $p$ be a prime, let $n\ge0$, and let $(K,\mathcal O,k)$ be a splitting
$p$-modular system for $S_n$, so that $k$ is a splitting field of
characteristic $p$ for $S_n$
([[def-splitting-p-modular-system-for-a-finite-group]]). For $\mu\vdash n$
write $S^\mu_k=k\otimes_{\mathbb Z}S^\mu_{\mathbb Z}$ for the field-valued
Specht module, $D^\mu=S^\mu_k/R^\mu$ for its modular form quotient
([[def-modular-specht-form-and-radical-quotient]]), and let
$$S(\mu):=(S^\mu_k)^*=\operatorname{Hom}_k(S^\mu_k,k),\qquad (\sigma\cdot f)(x):=f(\sigma^{-1}x)$$
be the **dual Specht module**, with
$$D(\mu):=\operatorname{hd}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr) =S(\mu)/\operatorname{rad}\bigl(S(\mu)\bigr)$$
its head ([[def-module-radical-socle-head-and-loewy-series]]). Let
$\mu'$ be the conjugate partition, and let
$S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$ be the tensor product of
$k[S_n]$-modules with the diagonal action
$\sigma\cdot(x\otimes w)=(\sigma\cdot x)\otimes(\sigma\cdot w)$, where
$\operatorname{sgn}$ is the one-dimensional sign representation
([[def-sign-representation-and-restriction-of-a-representation]],
[[def-tensor-product-of-modules-by-generators-and-relations]]).

1. **Dual Specht versus sign-twisted conjugate.** If $\mu$ is $p$-restricted
   (equivalently, by
   [[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]], $\mu'$ is $p$-regular),
   then $S(\mu)\cong S^{\mu'}_k\otimes\operatorname{sgn}$; consequently
   $S(\mu)$ is nonzero with simple head
   $$D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}\otimes\operatorname{sgn},$$
   a nonzero simple $k[S_n]$-module that is self-dual and absolutely
   irreducible.
2. **Equivalent form for $p$-regular labels.** If $\lambda\vdash n$ is
   $p$-regular, then $\lambda'$ is $p$-restricted and
   $$D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')\otimes\operatorname{sgn}.$$
3. **The two labellings.** The map $\mu\mapsto D(\mu)$ is a bijection from
   the set of $p$-restricted partitions of $n$ to the set of isomorphism
   classes of simple $k[S_n]$-modules; that is, every simple
   $k[S_n]$-module is isomorphic to $D(\mu)$ for exactly one $p$-restricted
   $\mu\vdash n$.

In characteristic $2$ the sign representation is the trivial representation,
so the formulas read $D(\mu)\cong D^{\mu'}$ and $D^\lambda\cong D(\lambda')$;
the transposition is still required, and the two labellings coincide only
for self-conjugate partitions. No step divides by a group order or uses
averaging, and $n=0$ is included.

- Its **radical** is

  formed using [[def-quotient-module]].

- Its **Loewy series** is the descending radical filtration
  $$   M\supseteq \operatorname{rad}(M)\supseteq \operatorname{rad}^2(M)\supseteq\cdots   $$
  together with the corresponding semisimple layers

$\tilde e_i,\tilde f_i$ for $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ by
$$\tilde e_i\mu:=\mu\setminus A\quad\text{if }\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $A$ is the good $i$-node of $\mu$
([[def-residue-signature-normal-good-conormal-and-cogood-nodes]]), the
operator being undefined on $\mu$ when $\varepsilon_i(\mu)=0$; and
$$\tilde f_i\mu:=\mu\cup B\quad\text{if }\varphi_i(\mu)>0,$$
where $B$ is the cogood $i$-node of $\mu$, the operator being undefined on
$\mu$ when $\varphi_i(\mu)=0$. Then
$$\mu=\tilde f_i\nu\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad\nu=\tilde e_i\mu$$
for all $p$-restricted $\mu,\nu$; in particular $\tilde e_i$ and $\tilde f_i$
are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one
and each $\tilde f_i$ raises the rank by one, and at most one good and at most
one cogood node exist in each residue. No module-theoretic statement is made
here: this item is pure combinatorics, and the identification of these
operators with the crystal operators of the level-one Fock space is a theorem
of the later Fock-space page, not an input here.

Let $p>0$ and let $\mu$ be a $p$-restricted partition, so that
$\mu_i-\mu_{i+1}<p$ for all $i\ge1$
([[def-p-regular-and-p-restricted-partitions]],
[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]). A node $(r,c)$ of
the Young diagram $[\mu]$ is an **$i$-node** if its residue
$$\operatorname{res}(r,c):=c-r\bmod p$$
equals $i\in\mathbb Z/p$; the $i$-nodes of $\mu$ are its addable and removable
nodes of residue $i$
([[def-removable-and-addable-nodes-of-a-partition]]).

**The reduced $i$-signature.** Fix $i\in\mathbb Z/p$ and list the $i$-nodes
of $\mu$ as $A_1,\dots,A_n$ from top to bottom, that is, in increasing row
index and, for equal row index, in increasing column index. Form the word
$\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n)$ with $\sigma_m=+$ if $A_m$ is addable and
$\sigma_m=-$ if $A_m$ is removable. Whenever $r<s$, $\sigma_r=-$,
$\sigma_s=+$ and $\sigma_{r+1}=\dots=\sigma_{s-1}=0$, replace $\sigma_r$ and
$\sigma_s$ by $0$; repeat until no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$. The
resulting **reduced $i$-signature** has the form $+\cdots+- \cdots-$ with the
zeros deleted, and the nodes attached to its signs are:

- the **normal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the removable nodes corresponding to
  the $-$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **good $i$-node** is the topmost (first listed) of the normal $i$-nodes;
- the **conormal $i$-nodes** of $\mu$ are the addable nodes corresponding to
  the $+$ signs of the reduced signature;
- the **cogood $i$-node** is the bottommost (last listed) of the conormal
  $i$-nodes.

Write $\varepsilon_i(\mu)$ and $\varphi_i(\mu)$ for the numbers of normal and
of conormal $i$-nodes of $\mu$; the good $i$-node exists exactly when
$\varepsilon_i(\mu)>0$, and the cogood $i$-node exactly when
$\varphi_i(\mu)>0$. At most one good and at most one cogood $i$-node occur,
for each residue.

sequence of steps terminates after at most $\lfloor n/2\rfloor$ steps, and in
the resulting word no $-$ lies to the left of a $+$: otherwise, take two
nonzero entries that are consecutive among the nonzero entries of the current
word and are ordered $-$, $+$; all entries strictly between them are $0$ by
the choice, so the pair would still be reducible. Hence a terminal word is
$+^a0^c-^b$ for some $a,b,c\ge0$. The terminal word does not depend on the
order in which reducible pairs are chosen: two reducible pairs cannot overlap
partially, because an endpoint of one pair lying strictly inside the other
would be a nonzero entry in a position that the other pair requires to be
$0$, and pairs sharing exactly one endpoint would similarly place a nonzero
entry strictly inside the other pair; so any two reducible pairs are either
disjoint (and the corresponding steps commute) or equal, there are no
critical pairs, and the rewriting relation is locally confluent. A
terminating and locally confluent rewriting relation is confluent, so the
terminal word is unique; in it the first surviving $-$ and the last surviving
$+$ are unique positions whenever they exist. Thus the reduced signature,
the sets of normal and conormal nodes, and the good and cogood nodes are well
defined. The empty partition has no $i$-nodes and empty signature, with
$\varepsilon_i(\varnothing)=\varphi_i(\varnothing)=0$ for all $i$.

Brundan's $\ell$-residue $r-c$, and a removable node of $\mu$ is normal here
exactly when its transposed node is normal in Brundan's sense for the
transpose partition $\mu'$; lists of addable and removable nodes, and the
signs of the residues, must never be silently mixed between the two
conventions

[[def-partition-young-diagram-and-conjugate-partition]]).

are mutual inverses on their domains, each $\tilde e_i$ lowers the rank by one

Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $p>0$. Every $p$-restricted partition
$\mu$ of $d$ is obtained from the empty partition by $d$ successive cogood
additions: there are residues $i_1,\dots,i_d$ with
$$\mu=\tilde f_{i_d}\cdots\tilde f_{i_1}\varnothing;$$
equivalently, every $p$-restricted $\mu\ne\varnothing$ has at least one good

([[def-good-node-and-cogood-node-crystal-operators]],

the graph whose vertices are the $p$-restricted partitions and whose edges
join $\nu$ to $\tilde f_i\nu$ for every $i$ for which the operator is
defined, the empty partition is the unique vertex of rank $0$ and every
vertex is reached from it; dually every vertex reaches the empty partition by
successive good deletions. The argument is choice-free.

By [F2] the socle of $D^{\lambda}\downarrow_{H(r-1)}$ is the sum of the two simple modules $D^{\lambda(1)}=D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}$ and $D^{\lambda(5)}=D^{(6,4,4,3,1)}$ attached to the two good rows, and these two simples lie in pairwise different blocks of $H(r-1)$; a direct sum of modules in different blocks has more than one nonzero summand, so the restriction is decomposable.

$\ell=4$: indecomposability. By [F2] the socle of $D^{\lambda}\downarrow_{H(r-1)}$ is the single simple module $D^{\lambda(1)}=D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}$, occurring with multiplicity one; the restriction is self-dual by [F3], so its head is the dual of its socle, again the same simple module, and a module with simple socle occurring once is indecomposable, since a nontrivial decomposition would exhibit the socle as the direct sum of the socles of two nonzero summands.

The example as a convention stress test. The computed tables show that the residue list alone does not determine normality: at $\ell=4$ row $4$ has the same residue as rows $1,3,5$ yet fails the lattice test $\{5\}\not\downarrow\varnothing$, so it is not normal; and good rows are the minimal normal rows per residue, not the removable rows whose residue occurs once. The two conclusions, decomposable at $\ell=3$ and indecomposable at $\ell=4$, follow from the socle theorem and the block separation recorded in [F2], as verified in steps 4.1 and 4.2; the $\ell=4$ socle label is $D^{(5,4,4,3,2)}=D^{\lambda(1)}$.

Let $R$ be a commutative ring with $1$ and $A$ a unital $R$-algebra
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]) that is free as an $R$-module on a
finite set $C=\{c^{\lambda}_{st}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ s,t\in T(\lambda)\}$,
where $(\Lambda,\unrhd)$ is a finite poset ([[def-partial-order]]; its strict
order is written $\rhd$) and each $T(\lambda)$ is a finite set. For
$\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ be the $R$-submodule of $A$ spanned
by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with $\mu\rhd\lambda$.

Then $(C,\Lambda)$ is a **cellular basis** of $A$, and $A$ is a **cellular
algebra**, if:

(i) the $R$-linear map $i:A\to A$ with $i(c^{\lambda}_{st})=c^{\lambda}_{ts}$
for all $\lambda,s,t$ is an algebra anti-automorphism of $A$, i.e. $i(ab)=i(b)i(a)$
and $i(1)=1$ (equivalently $i$ is an isomorphism of $A$ with the opposite
algebra; the displayed formula forces $i^2=\mathrm{id}$); and

(ii) for every $\lambda\in\Lambda$, every $t\in T(\lambda)$ and every $a\in A$
there exist $r_v\in R$ ($v\in T(\lambda)$) with
$$c^{\lambda}_{st}\,a\equiv\sum_{v\in T(\lambda)}r_v\,c^{\lambda}_{sv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}.$$

**Cell modules.** For $\lambda\in\Lambda$ let $C^{\lambda}$ be the free
$R$-module with basis $\{c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_{tt}:t\in T(\lambda)\}$;
condition (ii) makes $C^{\lambda}$ a right $A$-module by
$c^{\lambda}_t a:=\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_v$ when
$c^{\lambda}_{tt}a\equiv\sum_v r_vc^{\lambda}_{tv}\pmod{A^{\rhd\lambda}}$, and
it makes $C^{\lambda}$ a left $A$-module via $i$, the left action being
$a\cdot c^{\lambda}_t:=c^{\lambda}_t\,i(a)$. Both actions are well defined on
the freely spanning basis elements by (ii): the coefficients $r_v$ are unique
because $C$ is an $R$-basis of $A$ and the quotient by $A^{\rhd\lambda}$ kills
exactly the basis elements indexed by strictly larger labels, while applying
the anti-automorphism (i) to (ii) gives the same triangularity for left
multiplication. The module $C^{\lambda}$ is the **(right) cell module** of
$\lambda$, and
$$A^{\unrhd\lambda}/A^{\rhd\lambda}\cong C^{\lambda}\otimes_R C^{\lambda}$$
via $c^{\lambda}_{st}+A^{\rhd\lambda}\mapsto c^{\lambda}_s\otimes c^{\lambda}_t$,
where $A^{\unrhd\lambda}$ is spanned by all $c^{\mu}_{uv}$ with
$\mu\unrhd\lambda$. A cellular algebra may have several cellular bases.

Let $F$ be a field and $A$ a finite-dimensional unital cellular $F$-algebra with
cellular basis $(C,\Lambda)$ over the finite poset $\Lambda$
([[def-cellular-algebra-basis-and-cell-module]]). For $\lambda\in\Lambda$
put $D^{\lambda}:=C^{\lambda}/\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$, where
$\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the radical of the cell form
([[lem-cell-form-is-associative-and-its-radical-is-a-submodule]]). Then:

1. if $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ then $D^{\lambda}$ is an absolutely irreducible
   (absolutely simple) $A$-module: it is simple over $F$ and remains simple
   after every extension of scalars to a larger field;
2. $\{D^{\lambda}:\lambda\in\Lambda,\ D^{\lambda}\ne0\}$ is a complete set of
   pairwise non-isomorphic simple $A$-modules ([[def-simple-module]],
   [[thm-jordan-holder-theorem-for-modules]]);
3. $D^{\lambda}\ne0$ if and only if the cell form
   $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_\lambda$ is not identically zero, if and only if
   $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}\ne C^{\lambda}$; and, when these equivalent
   conditions hold, $\mathrm{rad}\,C^{\lambda}$ is the unique maximal proper
   submodule and the Jacobson radical of $C^{\lambda}$, so $D^{\lambda}$ is its
   simple head. If the form is identically zero, the cell-form quotient
   $D^{\lambda}$ is zero; no assertion about the Jacobson radical or the actual
   head of $C^{\lambda}$ is made.

No semisimplicity of $A$ is assumed; the theorem is the Graham-Lehrer
classification and applies in particular to $A=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ for every field
$F$ and every $q\in F^{\times}$.

derivations.claim: Extend only to $K=F(t)$. This field is infinite, and extension preserves the rank of every finite Gram matrix. A nonzero Schur cell-form quotient stays simple after this extension: in any field a vector outside its radical generates the entire cell module by the cellular rank-one action, and the same argument applies to the extended nonzero Gram form. No algebraic closure or infinite-choice step is required.

At $q=1$, identify $ igoplus _
u M^
u$ with the tensorword basis of $(K^N)^{\otimes m}, m=|\mu |$, by sending $m_
u T_{d}$ to the word whose $j$th letter is the row containing entry $j$ in the row-standard tableau $t^
u d$. This is the explicit right-coset/tensorword convention; for regular type and basis $d$, that letter is $j d^{-1}$ under right permutation notation. The symmetric-group action on tensor positions is transported through this map, so inverses in labels and right-position actions are fixed consistently. The symmetric group permutes the tensor positions. An endomorphism commuting with this permutation action has matrix coefficients constant on its orbits on pairs of words. Such orbits are indexed by nonnegative integer matrices $A=(A_{ab})$ with $\sum A_{ab}=m$, recording the number of positions with input $b$ and output $a$. Let $E_{A}$ be the matrix with entry 1 on that orbit and 0 elsewhere. The $E_{A}$ have disjoint support and form a basis of the endomorphism algebra. For a matrix $g$, $g^{\otimes m}=\sum _{A} (\prod _{ab} g_{ab}^{A_{ab}})E_{A}$. The transpose involution sends $E_{A}$ to $E_{A^T}$; it is precisely the $q=1$ Schur star (the corresponding semistandard Hom maps are transposes under the orthonormal tensorword/permutation forms).

Invertible-matrix evaluations span this Schur algebra over $K$. Indeed a linear functional annihilating all $g^{\otimes m}$ gives a polynomial $P(g)=\sum _{A} c_{A} g^A$ vanishing whenever $\det(g)\ne 0$. Then $P\det$ vanishes at every matrix over $K$. An elementary induction on the number of variables shows that a polynomial over an infinite field vanishing everywhere is zero: regard it as a polynomial in the last variable and use infinitely many values, then apply the induction to its coefficients. Thus $P\det=0$ as a polynomial, and the polynomial domain gives $P=0$, so all $c_{A}$ vanish. Finite-dimensional duality proves the spanning claim. Consequently the star-converted Schur simple is a simple rational left $\operatorname{GL}_N$-module, with the same submodules and composition multiplicities as the right Schur module.

The canonical semistandard tableau has weight $\mu$ and Schur form value 1. Indeed its diagonal Schur basis element is the projection onto the permutation summand $M^\mu $: the defining Hom map is the identity there and zero on the other summands. Its square is itself, so the defining cell-product coefficient, which is the canonical tableau norm, is 1. This argument uses the canonical diagonal projection only, not an idempotence assertion for all diagonal tableau elements. Every semistandard tableau weight $\nu$ is dominated by $\mu $: for each $k$, all entries $\le k$ occur in the first $k$ rows by column strictness, so there are at most $\mu _{1}+\cdots +\mu _{k}$ of them. The unique tableau of weight $\mu$ is the canonical one. Thus $L$ has highest weight $\mu$ with one-dimensional highest space $K v$, and its positive upper unipotent group fixes $v$: any nonconstant positive-root coefficient would have weight strictly above $\mu$. Torus weights are integer characters, distinct as Laurent monomials over $K$; no Lie-eigenvalue congruence substitutes for weight equality.

On the open set where leading principal minors are nonzero, Gaussian elimination gives $g=u^- d u^+$. The negative-unipotent coefficient operators on $v$ span $L$. To see this, let $W$ be their span and let $\ell$ annihilate $W$. Then $\ell (gv)=0$ on that open set because $u^+v=v$ and $dv$ is a scalar multiple of $v$. A polynomial matrix coefficient vanishing there vanishes identically by the same polynomial-identity argument, so $\ell$ annihilates the coefficient orbit of $v$ under all $\operatorname{GL}_{N}$. That orbit spans $L$ by simplicity. Hence $W=L$.

Positive coefficient operators detect every nonzero vector $x$ of weight $\mu -\gamma$. If they all had zero highest coefficient on $x$, the Gaussian factorization would imply that the highest coefficient of $gx$ was zero on the same open set: negative operators cannot raise a weight to $\mu$, and no weight exceeds $\mu$. The resulting polynomial identity would make that coefficient zero on the whole simple-module orbit of $x$, which spans $L$ and contains $v$, a contradiction. Thus some positive coefficient operator of weight $\gamma$ raises $x$ to a nonzero multiple of $v$.

For $\gamma =\alpha (r,s)$, every simple-root coefficient is 1. In a product expansion of a unipotent matrix, any monomial of total root weight $\gamma$ therefore has each root-variable exponent $0$ or $1$, and its roots are pairwise disjoint intervals covering $[r,s]$. They are exactly cut partitions of that interval. Put  $f_{a,b}=E_{b+1,a}, e_{i}=E_{i,i+1}, Y_{r,s}(U)=f_{r,u_{1}-1}f_{u_{1},u_{2}-1}\cdots f_{u_{k},s}$, for $U=\{u_{1}<\cdots <u_{k}\}\subset (r,s]$, with $Y(\varnothing )=f_{r,s}$. These words span the required negative coefficient space. Similarly the positive coefficient space is spanned by words using each $e_{r},\cdots ,e_{s}$ once. Root-matrix commutators expand every longer positive root into such simple words. Permutations of these simple letters are identified using $e_{i} e_{j}=e_{j} e_{i}$ for $|i-j|>1$; their relative orders on adjacent pairs determine the canonical representative  $Q_{r,s}(I)=e_{i_{k}}\cdots e_{i_{1}} \cdot \prod _{j\in [r,s]\setminus I}^{\mathrm{increasing}}e_{j}, I=\{i_{1}<\cdots <i_{k}\}\subset (r,s]$. Every word is carried to this representative by exchanging adjacent incomparable letters in the corresponding path partial order. Hence these $Q$ words span all positive tests at the interval weight. There are no divided powers greater than 1 or factorial denominators in this grade.

The actions and all commutator calculations below use $[E_{ab},E_{cd}]=\delta _{bc} E_{ad} -\delta _{da} E_{cb}, e_{i} v=0$, and $(E_{ii} -E_{i+1,i+1})v=a_{i} v$. They are integral matrix identities and apply to the actual Schur module. The construction descends from $K$ to $F$ because the resulting matrices have entries in $F$ and scalar extension preserves all ranks and linear relations.

otin U$, put  $\zeta (M,U)=\zeta (M',U)/C(r,m)$. If $m\in U$, put  $\zeta (M,U)=[\zeta (M',U)-\zeta _{r,m-1}(\varnothing ,U\cap (r,m)) \zeta _{m,s}(M',U\cap (m,s])]/C(r,m)$. If $J$ has consecutive components $[\beta _{1},\gamma _{1}],\cdots ,[\beta _{q},\gamma _{q}]$, matrix commutation and $(T)$ give, for $i<s, e_{i} T_{r,s}(J)v=0$ unless $i=\beta _{a}-1$ for some $a$;  $e_{\beta _{a}-1}T_{r,s}(J)v =-T_{r,\beta _{a}-2}(J\cap (r,\beta _{a}-1)) T_{\beta _{a},s}((\beta _{a},\gamma _{a}]\cup \bigcup _{b>a}[\beta _{b},\gamma _{b}])v$.                  $(X)$ Empty prefix operators are interpreted as 1. These formulas follow directly as follows. In the empty-$J$ expansion, group $Y$ words by membership of $i$ and $i+1$ in their cuts. The coefficient of each residual word cancels through  $-C(r,i+1)+C(r,i)+(a_{i}+1)=0$ for $i<s$. At the endpoint the two contributions are $C(r,s)$ and $a_{s}$, whose sum is $B(r,s)$, giving $(E)$. At $i=m-1$, the first term has zero action; on the product term the empty-prefix endpoint coefficient is $B(r,m-1)+1=C(r,m)$, since the later negative interval increases its adjacent Cartan value by 1. For later component starts the positive operator commutes with the initial prefix, and applying the induction to both terms in $(T)$ is exactly the same $(T)$ recursion for the shorter first factor in $(X)$. The stronger identity, for $m=\min J$ (and $m=s+1$ when $J=\varnothing$), is  $\Xi _{r,s}(J)=\prod _{t\in [r,s]\setminus D}B(r,t) +[\prod _{t=r}^{m-1}B(r,t)] \sum _{j\in J}B(j,d(j))P_{j}(C(r,m))$, where each $P_{j}$ has integer-polynomial coefficients independent of $r$. The two induction formulas for $J\setminus \{m\}$, starting respectively at $r$ and $m$, have exactly the same $P_{j}$. Their left factors differ by replacing each $b_{t}$ with $x+b_{t}$. Substitute them into $(C)$, factoring $A=\prod _{t=r}^{m-1}B(r,t)$. The principal numerator is  $\prod _{t\in [m,s]\setminus D'}(x+b_{t})-\prod _{t\in [m,s]\setminus D'}b_{t} =x \prod _{t\in [m,s]\setminus D}(x+b_{t}) +b_{v}[\prod _{t\in [m,s]\setminus D}(x+b_{t})-\prod _{t\in [m,s]\setminus D}b_{t}]$. The bracket on the second line is divisible by $x$ in the integer polynomial ring.
